title: Deep Clone
description: Recursively clone plain objects and arrays so mutating the clone never touches the original — the canonical recursion + WeakMap-for-cycles pattern.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down what 'clone' means.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: `deepClone(value)` returns a new value where mutating the clone never touches the original — independent at every level of nesting. Quick clarifying questions:"

• Scope — just plain objects + arrays + primitives, or do I also need Date / Map / Set / RegExp / class instances?
• Cycles — can the input have cyclic references (an object pointing back to itself)? If yes, infinite recursion is a real failure mode.
• Functions — if a property is a function, do I copy the reference, skip it, or throw?
• Symbol keys — `Object.keys` skips them. Should I use `Reflect.ownKeys` to include them?
• Non-enumerable / getters / prototype chain — full structural clone, or just own-enumerable string-keyed properties?
sections.why: The scope question is the load-bearing one — interviewers almost always answer "plain objects + arrays + primitives, you can ignore Date/Map/Set", which collapses the problem to the recursive-WeakMap version. But asking it signals you know `structuredClone` exists and handles more, and you're choosing the simpler problem deliberately. The cycle question is the structural one — if cycles are in scope, you need a `seen` registry; if not, you can skip it. Asking both upfront prevents writing the wrong solution.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the one-liner that almost works.
sections.say:
"The one-liner is `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(value))`. It deep-copies plain JSON-shaped data in a single line. But it has real failure modes I'd want to flag:"

• Drops functions, `undefined`, and Symbols silently.
• Converts `Date` to a string, `Map`/`Set` to `{}`, `RegExp` to `{}`.
• Throws on cycles (`Converting circular structure to JSON`).
• Loses class prototype info — every clone becomes a plain object.

"For a true interview implementation, I want explicit recursion so I can control these. Let me build it."
sections.why: Naming `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(x))` first is the right move because (a) it's the production answer for 90% of real cases, (b) listing its failure modes proves you know WHY it's not sufficient, and (c) it gives the interviewer a chance to scope the problem down ("that's fine for now, ship it") or up ("build the real one"). Skipping it and going straight to recursion makes you look like you don't know the easy answer.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What's the recursion shape, and what makes cycles hard?
sections.say:
"This is structural recursion over the value graph. At each node: if primitive (including `null`) — return it as-is, no copy needed. If array — allocate a new array, recurse each element. If object — allocate a new object, recurse each property. The recursion bottoms out at primitives."

"The cycle wrinkle is the load-bearing one. If `a.self = a`, naïve recursion descends into `a.self`, sees `a`, recurses into THAT `a.self`, forever. The fix: maintain a `WeakMap` from source-node → in-progress-clone-node. Before recursing into a node's children, register the empty clone in the map. Then when a child encounters the same source node, it finds the in-progress clone and returns it — cycle preserved, recursion bounded. The 'register BEFORE recursing' is the critical ordering."
sections.why: Articulating the register-before-recurse ordering is the test — anyone who registers AFTER the recursion still infinite-loops on cycles. Calling out WeakMap specifically (vs. plain Map) shows you understand why: WeakMap holds keys weakly, so the cache doesn't prevent the source graph from being garbage-collected after `deepClone` returns. The primitive-as-base-case framing also makes the recursion feel mathematically clean rather than ad-hoc.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model.
sections.intro: "Let me trace three cases — a nested object to show recursion, a flat array to show the array branch, and a single-key object as the trivial case."

examples.note: Two-level nested — recursion goes 3 levels deep (root → b → c → primitives).
examples.trace:
visit root  → object, allocate {}. register seen.set(root, out).
  visit root.a=1     → primitive, return 1. out={a:1}
  visit root.b={c:[1,2]} → object, allocate {}. register seen.set(root.b, innerOut).
    visit root.b.c=[1,2] → array, allocate []. register seen.set(root.b.c, arrOut).
      visit [0]=1 → primitive, return 1. arrOut=[1]
      visit [1]=2 → primitive, return 2. arrOut=[1,2]
    innerOut={c:[1,2]}
  out={a:1, b:{c:[1,2]}} ✓ independent at every level

examples.note: Array branch — Array.isArray(value) routes us to [], not {}.
examples.trace:
visit root → Array.isArray=true, allocate []. register seen.set(root, arrOut).
  visit [0]=10 → primitive, return 10. arrOut=[10]
  visit [1]=20 → primitive, return 20. arrOut=[10,20]
  visit [2]=30 → primitive, return 30. arrOut=[10,20,30]
return [10,20,30] ✓ — and arrOut !== root

examples.note: Trivial — one primitive child, no recursion into objects.

sections.why: Tracing the nested case surfaces the recursion-depth bug: if you forgot to recurse and just did `out[k] = value[k]`, `out.b` would point at the SAME object as `value.b`, and mutating `out.b.c` would corrupt the original. The array example confirms the `Array.isArray` branch — without it, arrays would clone as objects with numeric string keys, breaking `.length` and any array methods. Walking through these on the whiteboard is how you catch both.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would break a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:"

• Cycles (`a.self = a`) — the register-before-recurse pattern handles this; without it, stack overflow.
• `null` — `typeof null === 'object'`, so the primitive guard must check `value === null` explicitly or null inputs recurse and crash on `Object.keys(null)`.
• `Date` / `Map` / `Set` / `RegExp` — the recursive version copies these as `{}` because `Object.keys(new Date())` is empty. For a full solution, branch on `instanceof Date` → `new Date(value)`, on Map/Set → reconstruct, on RegExp → `new RegExp(value.source, value.flags)`.
• Symbol keys — `Object.keys` skips them. Use `Reflect.ownKeys(value)` if Symbol keys must survive.
• Functions as property values — typically copy the reference (functions are immutable-as-references; deep-cloning a function isn't meaningful).
• Null-prototype objects (`Object.create(null)`) — the clone uses `{}` which has `Object.prototype`. If prototype identity matters, use `Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(value))`.
• Non-enumerable / getters — `Object.keys` skips non-enumerables, and reading a getter triggers it. For a faithful clone, use `Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptors` + `Object.defineProperties`.
sections.why: The `null` edge is the one that bites everyone — `typeof null === 'object'` is a well-known JS quirk, and forgetting the explicit null check produces an `Object.keys(null)` crash on the first null property. The Symbol-keys and getter callouts are the senior-tier signals — most candidates don't think about them, and the interviewer either says "good catch, assume own-enumerable string keys only" (which is the standard scope) or asks you to handle them (which becomes the harder follow-up).

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the bounds, and what does this generalize to?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) where n is the total number of nodes in the value graph (every property at every depth). Each node is visited exactly once because the `seen` WeakMap short-circuits revisits — that's the same amortization argument as cycle detection in graph traversal, just over the property graph.

Space is also O(n) — the WeakMap holds one entry per visited node, plus the recursion stack which is O(depth). For typical object graphs depth is small, but for an adversarial linked-list-shaped object you'd want an iterative version to avoid stack overflow.

If you wanted me to extend: the production answer in modern environments is `structuredClone(value)` — a built-in browser API that handles Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, typed arrays, and cycles, and is faster than a JS implementation. The recursive version we just wrote is the right interview answer (proves you understand the recursion shape); `structuredClone` is the right production answer."
sections.why: The 'visit each node once because WeakMap short-circuits' argument is the amortization defense — without it, an interviewer could push back with "what if the same subtree is referenced from two places?" Naming `structuredClone` unprompted is the senior signal: it shows you know what the platform already gives you and chose the manual implementation because it was the question, not because you didn't know the easier path.

walkthrough.intro: Step through deepClone on a nested object. The trace simulates the recursion as an explicit stack of paths — each yield shows the current path being copied, the clone built so far, and the `seen` registry. Cycle examples demonstrate why we register-before-recursing.

examples.label: { a: 1, b: { c: [1,2] } } → independent deep copy

trace: yield { line: 1, label: `enter deepClone — value=${JSON.stringify(input)}, seen=new WeakMap()`, state: { input, seen: [] } };
yield { line: 2, label: `visit path '${path}' — typeof=${value === null ? 'null' : Array.isArray(value) ? 'array' : typeof value}`, state: { path, value, seen: [...seen.keys()].map((_, i) => i) } };
yield { line: 2, label: `primitive '${JSON.stringify(value)}' — return as-is`, state: { path, value, returns_subtree: value } };
yield { line: 4, label: `cycle hit at '${path}' — return registered in-progress clone`, state: { path, value, seen: [...seen.keys()].map((_, i) => i) } };
yield { line: 6, label: `allocate empty ${Array.isArray(value) ? 'array' : 'object'} for '${path}'`, state: { path, value, out: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(out)) } };
yield { line: 8, label: `register '${path}' in seen BEFORE recursing (cycle safety)`, state: { path, value, out: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(out)), seenSize: seen.size } };
yield { line: 9, label: `recurse into '${path}.${k}'`, state: { path, k, parent: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(out)) } };
yield { line: 9, label: `assigned out['${k}'] — '${path}' so far: ${JSON.stringify(out)}`, state: { path, k, out: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(out)) } };
yield { line: 10, label: `done with '${path}' — return ${JSON.stringify(out)}`, state: { path, out: JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(out)) } };
yield { line: 10, label: `top-level return — clone=${JSON.stringify(result)}`, state: { input, clone: result, returns: JSON.stringify(result) } };

notes: Primitives (number, string, boolean, null, undefined) are immutable — return as-is, no copy needed.
Register the new object in the WeakMap before recursing into children, or cyclic graphs recurse forever.
This minimal version skips Date, Map, Set, RegExp, and class prototypes. Real `structuredClone` handles those; interviews usually only ask for the recursive core.
Time O(n) where n = total nodes. Space O(n) for the clone + WeakMap + recursion stack.

alternates.label: structuredClone (built-in, production answer)
alternates.when: Use in production code when you're targeting Node 17+ or modern browsers — it handles Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer, typed arrays, and cyclic references natively and is faster than a JS implementation. The recursive version in the primary is what an interviewer wants (shows you understand the algorithm); structuredClone is what you'd ship in real code.
notes: structuredClone is a W3C standard built into browsers (Chrome 98+, Node 17+) — no library needed.
Handles cycles, Date, Map, Set, ArrayBuffer; throws on functions, DOM nodes, and class instances that aren't serializable.
Prefer this in production; use the recursive version in interviews to demonstrate you understand the algorithm.

alternates.label: JSON round-trip (JSON.parse + JSON.stringify)
alternates.when: Acceptable for plain JSON-shaped data where you know there are no functions, undefined values, Date objects, cycles, or class instances. It is the one-liner answer — name it first to show you know it, then explain why the recursive version is correct for the general case.
notes: Silently drops functions, undefined, and Symbol keys — the clone will be missing those properties entirely.
Converts Date to ISO string, Map/Set/RegExp to {} — prototypes are lost.
Throws on cyclic references (circular structure); use the recursive+WeakMap version or structuredClone for those.

questions.q: Why must you set `seen.set(value, out)` before iterating the object's keys?
options: Reads in WeakMap return stale values until a write commits, so it primes the cache
To handle cycles: a child that references back to value must find the in-progress clone
Setting after the loop overwrites the populated children with the empty `out`
Otherwise `seen.has(value)` short-circuits the recursion before children are copied
questions.explain: For `cyc.self = cyc`, the recursion into `self` re-enters with the same object; registering `out` first means that call hits `seen.has` and returns the half-built clone instead of recursing forever. Registering after the key loop would blow the stack on any cycle — the loop never gets to finish.

`typeof 42 !== 'object'` so the first guard returns it untouched — primitives are immutable, so sharing one is indistinguishable from copying it. That guard also carries `null`, which has to be tested explicitly because `typeof null === 'object'`.

questions.q: After `const b = deepClone(a); b.nested.x = 99;`, why is `a.nested.x` unchanged?
options: Spread `{...a}` would copy `nested` by reference, but deepClone returns a structuredClone-backed proxy
Because `b.nested` is a new object, distinct from `a.nested`
Because the WeakMap pins the original so writes to `b` are rerouted to a new sub-object
Because `Object.assign` copies values, and deepClone is built on top of it
questions.explain: The recursion hit `a.nested`, took the `Array.isArray ? [] : {}` branch and rebuilt it, so `b.nested` is a fresh object and the write lands only there. `{...a}` or `Object.assign` would have copied the `nested` POINTER, and this exact mutation would show up on the original.

questions.q: Why WeakMap instead of Map for the `seen` cache?
options: Map keys are compared by `==`, so two equal objects would collide; WeakMap uses identity
WeakMap holds keys weakly, so the cache doesn't block GC of cloned graphs
WeakMap's `.has()` is O(1); Map's `.has()` is O(log n)
Map throws if a key is reassigned, which would fire when registering the clone
questions.explain: `seen` keys every source object it visits, and a plain Map would keep all of them alive for as long as the map lives — the standard leak when a cache is hoisted out of the call. Both keep keys by identity, so identity lookup is NOT the difference between them.
